Multivariate Analysis

4 Principal Components Analysis

R code for this chapter: pca_figures.R (data and figures) and _common.R (shared helpers). Save both in one folder and run source("pca_figures.R"); every figure is then one function call, as shown under the Code buttons.

Slides for this chapter: pca_slides.html (opens in a new tab; use the arrow keys to move between slides).

The Introduction wrote the data as unit-variance shocks moved by a matrix, \(\mathbf x_t=A\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\), and showed that many \(A\) fit the same data. This chapter first adds one more step to that story: shocks with units. Splitting \(A\) into a part that scales the shocks and a part that combines them puts the Introduction’s choices of \(A\) (Cholesky, symmetric root, structural, PCA) into one frame (Section 4.1). The rest of the chapter works out one of them, principal components analysis (PCA): how to find the components, whether to start from the covariance or the correlation matrix, how many components to keep, how to read and use them, and what they do and do not tell us.

The examples of the Introduction carry the first sections, with two variables so that every step can be drawn: education and earnings, roommates’ grades, the flights, and above all Coca-Cola and Pepsi sales. The six state indicators of Chapter 2 then show PCA with more variables.

Notation as in the Introduction. Each variable is measured as a deviation from its mean, so the observations \(\mathbf x_t\) (rows of the data matrix \(\mathbf X\), bold because they are vectors) are centred, and the structural form is

\[ \mathbf x_t=A\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t , \]

with uncorrelated, unit-variance shocks \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) and \(AA'=\Sigma\). In the Introduction \(\Sigma\) was known. With data it is not: it is estimated by the sample covariance matrix \(S\) (Chapter 3), so the \(A\) we compute satisfies \(AA'=S\) and is an estimate too, as is everything derived from it below (to keep the formulas light, we drop the hats).

4.1 Factors with units: \(A=\Gamma D\)

4.1.1 Shocks have no units

Each choice of \(A\) in the Introduction came with a story: a regression of earnings on education (Cholesky), roommates’ grades (symmetric root), the flights (a structural restriction), and Coke and Pepsi (PCA). In every story the shocks have variance one. A shock of one means “one standard deviation more than usual”, which is a convenient coordinate but not a measurement. A pilot reports headwind in km/h, a registrar reports a GPA, an economist reports years of schooling. To speak about the forces in such units, \(A\) needs one more step.

4.1.2 Scale, then combine

Split \(A\) into two steps,

\[ \mathbf f_t=D\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t,\qquad \mathbf x_t=\Gamma\,\mathbf f_t,\qquad\text{so}\qquad A=\Gamma D . \]

  1. \(D\) is diagonal. It scales each unit-variance shock into a factor with its own units. The factors are still uncorrelated, and their variances, the diagonal of \(D^2\), say how important each factor is.
  2. \(\Gamma\) says how the measured variables respond to one unit of each factor.

The covariance matrix becomes \(S=AA'=\Gamma D^2\Gamma'\): the factor variances \(D^2\), combined by \(\Gamma\).

The split is not unique. Doubling the unit of factor \(j\) (halving \(d_j\)) and doubling column \(j\) of \(\Gamma\) leaves \(A\) unchanged. So, on top of the restriction that picked \(A\), splitting it needs one more assumption per factor, a normalisation that fixes the unit in which the factor is measured. Each story of the Introduction suggests a natural one. In each figure below, the unit-variance shocks (left) are scaled by \(D\) into factors (middle), which \(\Gamma\) combines into the data (right); the arrows show what one standard deviation of each factor does, and one observation (orange) is followed through the layers.

4.1.3 Cholesky: a regression

Take years of education \(x_1\) and annual earnings \(x_2\) (in $1000). The Cholesky restriction of the Introduction is \(a_{12}=0\): education does not respond to the earnings shock. The natural normalisation measures each factor in the units of “its” variable, so \(\Gamma\) has ones on the diagonal:

\[ x_{t1}=f_{t1},\qquad x_{t2}=\beta f_{t1}+f_{t2},\qquad \Gamma=L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ \beta&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad D=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_1&0\\0&\sigma_u\end{pmatrix}. \]

The shocks are scaled into the explanatory variable and the residual, and \(L\) combines them into the two variables. Factor 1 is education, with standard deviation \(\sigma_1=2.5\) years. \(\beta=4\) is the regression slope, $4000 a year per year of education, and factor 2 is the earnings residual, in $1000, with standard deviation \(\sigma_u=15\). The Cholesky factor of the Introduction is \(LD\), and \(S=LD^2L'\) is known as the LDL\('\) decomposition.

fig_md <- function(X, M, D, f_lab, x_lab, f_sub = NULL, equal = FALSE, obs = NULL) {
  A <- M %*% D; X <- scale(X, scale = FALSE); E <- X %*% t(solve(A)); Fm <- E %*% D
  if (is.null(obs)) obs <- which.min((E[, 1] - 1.3)^2 + (E[, 2] - 1.4)^2)
  col_wk <- "#e6820e"
  arrows_of2 <- function(B) geom_segment(data = tibble(xend = B[1, ], yend = B[2, ], col = c(col_a1, col_a2)),
                                         aes(0, 0, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = I(col)), linewidth = 1.3,
                                         arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed"))
  pts <- function(P) list(geom_point(data = tibble(x = P[, 1], y = P[, 2]), aes(x, y), colour = "#6f7a8c",
                                     alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2),
                          geom_point(aes(x = P[obs, 1], y = P[obs, 2]), colour = col_wk, size = 3))
  rng <- function(P) { r <- 1.08 * max(abs(P)); c(-r, r) }
  p1 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(E) + arrows_of2(diag(2)) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-3.4, 3.4), ylim = c(-3.4, 3.4)) +
    labs(title = expression("Shocks "*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = "variance 1, no units",
         x = expression(epsilon[1]), y = expression(epsilon[2]))
  p2 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(Fm) + arrows_of2(D) +
    (if (equal) coord_equal(xlim = rng(Fm), ylim = rng(Fm)) else
      coord_cartesian(xlim = rng(Fm[, 1]), ylim = rng(Fm[, 2]))) +
    labs(title = expression("Factors "*bold(f)[t] == D*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = f_sub, x = f_lab[1], y = f_lab[2])
  p3 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(X) + arrows_of2(A) +
    (if (equal) coord_equal(xlim = rng(X), ylim = rng(X)) else
      coord_cartesian(xlim = rng(X[, 1]), ylim = rng(X[, 2]))) +
    labs(title = expression("Data "*bold(x)[t] == Gamma*bold(f)[t]*" = "*Gamma*italic(D)*bold(epsilon)[t]*" = "*italic(A)*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = "deviations from the means",
         x = x_lab[1], y = x_lab[2])
  step <- function(lab) ggplot() +
    annotate("segment", x = 0.05, xend = 0.95, y = 0.5, yend = 0.5, linewidth = 1.1,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
    annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.62, label = lab, size = 5.5, parse = TRUE) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) + theme_void()
  p1 + step("italic(D)") + p2 + step("Gamma") + p3 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 0.2, 1, 0.2, 1))
}

fig_md_chol <- function() fig_md(chol_X, chol_M, chol_D,
  f_lab = c("education (years)", "earnings residual ($1000)"), x_lab = c("education (years)", "earnings ($1000)"),
  f_sub = "the regressor and the residual")

# draw the figure
fig_md_chol()

4.1.4 Symmetric root: roommates

Two first-year students are paired at random, and each one’s GPA is affected by the other. The symmetric root of the Introduction is \(a_{12}=a_{21}\): neither roommate comes first. Normalise again with ones on the diagonal: factor \(j\) is student \(j\)’s own contribution to her GPA, her GPA before the peer effect, in GPA points, and the off-diagonal entries of \(\Gamma\) are the peer effects,

\[ x_{t1}=f_{t1}+\gamma_{12}f_{t2},\qquad x_{t2}=\gamma_{21}f_{t1}+f_{t2}. \]

Here \(d_j=a_{jj}\) and \(\gamma_{ij}=a_{ij}/a_{jj}\). In the example each student’s own contribution has standard deviation 0.5 GPA points, and every point of the roommate’s own contribution adds \(\gamma_{12}=\gamma_{21}=0.2\) points to one’s GPA. With equally variable students, the symmetric \(A\) means equal peer effects in both directions, which is what random pairing suggests.

fig_md <- function(X, M, D, f_lab, x_lab, f_sub = NULL, equal = FALSE, obs = NULL) {
  A <- M %*% D; X <- scale(X, scale = FALSE); E <- X %*% t(solve(A)); Fm <- E %*% D
  if (is.null(obs)) obs <- which.min((E[, 1] - 1.3)^2 + (E[, 2] - 1.4)^2)
  col_wk <- "#e6820e"
  arrows_of2 <- function(B) geom_segment(data = tibble(xend = B[1, ], yend = B[2, ], col = c(col_a1, col_a2)),
                                         aes(0, 0, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = I(col)), linewidth = 1.3,
                                         arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed"))
  pts <- function(P) list(geom_point(data = tibble(x = P[, 1], y = P[, 2]), aes(x, y), colour = "#6f7a8c",
                                     alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2),
                          geom_point(aes(x = P[obs, 1], y = P[obs, 2]), colour = col_wk, size = 3))
  rng <- function(P) { r <- 1.08 * max(abs(P)); c(-r, r) }
  p1 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(E) + arrows_of2(diag(2)) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-3.4, 3.4), ylim = c(-3.4, 3.4)) +
    labs(title = expression("Shocks "*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = "variance 1, no units",
         x = expression(epsilon[1]), y = expression(epsilon[2]))
  p2 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(Fm) + arrows_of2(D) +
    (if (equal) coord_equal(xlim = rng(Fm), ylim = rng(Fm)) else
      coord_cartesian(xlim = rng(Fm[, 1]), ylim = rng(Fm[, 2]))) +
    labs(title = expression("Factors "*bold(f)[t] == D*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = f_sub, x = f_lab[1], y = f_lab[2])
  p3 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(X) + arrows_of2(A) +
    (if (equal) coord_equal(xlim = rng(X), ylim = rng(X)) else
      coord_cartesian(xlim = rng(X[, 1]), ylim = rng(X[, 2]))) +
    labs(title = expression("Data "*bold(x)[t] == Gamma*bold(f)[t]*" = "*Gamma*italic(D)*bold(epsilon)[t]*" = "*italic(A)*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = "deviations from the means",
         x = x_lab[1], y = x_lab[2])
  step <- function(lab) ggplot() +
    annotate("segment", x = 0.05, xend = 0.95, y = 0.5, yend = 0.5, linewidth = 1.1,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
    annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.62, label = lab, size = 5.5, parse = TRUE) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) + theme_void()
  p1 + step("italic(D)") + p2 + step("Gamma") + p3 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 0.2, 1, 0.2, 1))
}

fig_md_room <- function() fig_md(room_X, room_M, room_D,
  f_lab = c("student 1's own GPA", "student 2's own GPA"), x_lab = c("GPA of student 1", "GPA of student 2"),
  f_sub = "GPA before the peer effect", equal = TRUE)

# draw the figure
fig_md_room()

4.1.5 Structural: the flights

The flights need outside information twice. First, to identify \(A\): the aircraft manual says that an extra minute at cruise burns 100 kg of fuel, which fixes the direction of the headwind column (Section 1.4). Second, to normalise the factors, one more fact for each:

  • Headwind in km/h. On this 640 km route at a cruise speed of 800 km/h, the flight takes \(640/(800-w)\) hours against a headwind of \(w\) km/h, so each extra km/h adds about \(640/800^2\) hours, or \(\gamma_{11}=0.06\) minutes.
  • Load in tonnes. The climb tables say that each extra tonne adds \(\gamma_{12}=0.1\) minutes.

With these two numbers the rest follows from \(A\): the factor standard deviations are \(d_1=a_{11}/\gamma_{11}=20\) km/h and \(d_2=a_{12}/\gamma_{12}=2\) tonnes, and the fuel row of \(\Gamma\) is \(\gamma_{21}=a_{21}/d_1\), 6 kg per km/h of headwind, and \(\gamma_{22}=a_{22}/d_2\), 65 kg per tonne:

\[ \underset{A}{\begin{pmatrix}1.20&0.20\\ 1.20&1.30\end{pmatrix}} =\underset{\Gamma}{\begin{pmatrix}0.06&0.1\\ 0.06&0.65\end{pmatrix}} \underset{D}{\begin{pmatrix}20&0\\ 0&2\end{pmatrix}}. \]

fig_md <- function(X, M, D, f_lab, x_lab, f_sub = NULL, equal = FALSE, obs = NULL) {
  A <- M %*% D; X <- scale(X, scale = FALSE); E <- X %*% t(solve(A)); Fm <- E %*% D
  if (is.null(obs)) obs <- which.min((E[, 1] - 1.3)^2 + (E[, 2] - 1.4)^2)
  col_wk <- "#e6820e"
  arrows_of2 <- function(B) geom_segment(data = tibble(xend = B[1, ], yend = B[2, ], col = c(col_a1, col_a2)),
                                         aes(0, 0, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = I(col)), linewidth = 1.3,
                                         arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed"))
  pts <- function(P) list(geom_point(data = tibble(x = P[, 1], y = P[, 2]), aes(x, y), colour = "#6f7a8c",
                                     alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2),
                          geom_point(aes(x = P[obs, 1], y = P[obs, 2]), colour = col_wk, size = 3))
  rng <- function(P) { r <- 1.08 * max(abs(P)); c(-r, r) }
  p1 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(E) + arrows_of2(diag(2)) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-3.4, 3.4), ylim = c(-3.4, 3.4)) +
    labs(title = expression("Shocks "*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = "variance 1, no units",
         x = expression(epsilon[1]), y = expression(epsilon[2]))
  p2 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(Fm) + arrows_of2(D) +
    (if (equal) coord_equal(xlim = rng(Fm), ylim = rng(Fm)) else
      coord_cartesian(xlim = rng(Fm[, 1]), ylim = rng(Fm[, 2]))) +
    labs(title = expression("Factors "*bold(f)[t] == D*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = f_sub, x = f_lab[1], y = f_lab[2])
  p3 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(X) + arrows_of2(A) +
    (if (equal) coord_equal(xlim = rng(X), ylim = rng(X)) else
      coord_cartesian(xlim = rng(X[, 1]), ylim = rng(X[, 2]))) +
    labs(title = expression("Data "*bold(x)[t] == Gamma*bold(f)[t]*" = "*Gamma*italic(D)*bold(epsilon)[t]*" = "*italic(A)*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = "deviations from the means",
         x = x_lab[1], y = x_lab[2])
  step <- function(lab) ggplot() +
    annotate("segment", x = 0.05, xend = 0.95, y = 0.5, yend = 0.5, linewidth = 1.1,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
    annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.62, label = lab, size = 5.5, parse = TRUE) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) + theme_void()
  p1 + step("italic(D)") + p2 + step("Gamma") + p3 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 0.2, 1, 0.2, 1))

4.1.6 PCA: Coke and Pepsi

PCA’s restriction is that the first column of \(A\) is as long as possible (Section 4.2 works it out). Its normalisation gives every column of \(\Gamma\) length one, \(\lVert\gamma_j\rVert=1\). Two things make this a clever choice:

  • One unit of a factor moves the observation by a distance of one, in the units of the data. A factor is a length along its direction, measured like the data themselves.
  • The variances add up. The total variance of the data (the sum of the variances, the trace of \(S\)) splits into the factor variances, \[ \operatorname{tr}(S)=\operatorname{tr}(\Gamma D^2\Gamma')=\sum_j d_j^2\,\lVert\gamma_j\rVert^2=\sum_j d_j^2 , \] so \(d_j^2\) is exactly the part of the total variance that factor \(j\) carries: nothing is gained or lost in the translation from factors to data.

Both only make sense when the variables share their units, a point Section 4.5 returns to. The PCA factors are called the principal component scores. Because they share the units of the data, the middle panel can be drawn to scale: the round cloud of shocks is stretched into an ellipse lined up with the axes, and \(\Gamma\) only turns it into place (Section 4.2). Read backwards, from the data to the shocks, the middle panel becomes the biplot of Section 4.2.

fig_md <- function(X, M, D, f_lab, x_lab, f_sub = NULL, equal = FALSE, obs = NULL) {
  A <- M %*% D; X <- scale(X, scale = FALSE); E <- X %*% t(solve(A)); Fm <- E %*% D
  if (is.null(obs)) obs <- which.min((E[, 1] - 1.3)^2 + (E[, 2] - 1.4)^2)
  col_wk <- "#e6820e"
  arrows_of2 <- function(B) geom_segment(data = tibble(xend = B[1, ], yend = B[2, ], col = c(col_a1, col_a2)),
                                         aes(0, 0, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = I(col)), linewidth = 1.3,
                                         arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed"))
  pts <- function(P) list(geom_point(data = tibble(x = P[, 1], y = P[, 2]), aes(x, y), colour = "#6f7a8c",
                                     alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2),
                          geom_point(aes(x = P[obs, 1], y = P[obs, 2]), colour = col_wk, size = 3))
  rng <- function(P) { r <- 1.08 * max(abs(P)); c(-r, r) }
  p1 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(E) + arrows_of2(diag(2)) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-3.4, 3.4), ylim = c(-3.4, 3.4)) +
    labs(title = expression("Shocks "*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = "variance 1, no units",
         x = expression(epsilon[1]), y = expression(epsilon[2]))
  p2 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(Fm) + arrows_of2(D) +
    (if (equal) coord_equal(xlim = rng(Fm), ylim = rng(Fm)) else
      coord_cartesian(xlim = rng(Fm[, 1]), ylim = rng(Fm[, 2]))) +
    labs(title = expression("Factors "*bold(f)[t] == D*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = f_sub, x = f_lab[1], y = f_lab[2])
  p3 <- ggplot() + axes0 + pts(X) + arrows_of2(A) +
    (if (equal) coord_equal(xlim = rng(X), ylim = rng(X)) else
      coord_cartesian(xlim = rng(X[, 1]), ylim = rng(X[, 2]))) +
    labs(title = expression("Data "*bold(x)[t] == Gamma*bold(f)[t]*" = "*Gamma*italic(D)*bold(epsilon)[t]*" = "*italic(A)*bold(epsilon)[t]), subtitle = "deviations from the means",
         x = x_lab[1], y = x_lab[2])
  step <- function(lab) ggplot() +
    annotate("segment", x = 0.05, xend = 0.95, y = 0.5, yend = 0.5, linewidth = 1.1,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
    annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.62, label = lab, size = 5.5, parse = TRUE) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) + theme_void()
  p1 + step("italic(D)") + p2 + step("Gamma") + p3 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 0.2, 1, 0.2, 1))
}

fig_md_cola <- function() {
  G <- cola_eig$vectors; if (G[1, 1] < 0) G[, 1] <- -G[, 1]; if (det(G) < 0) G[, 2] <- -G[, 2]
  fig_md(cola, G, diag(sqrt(cola_eig$values)), f_lab = c("score 1 (market)", "score 2 (brand switching)"),
         x_lab = c("Coca-Cola sales", "Pepsi sales"), f_sub = "lengths in the units of the data", equal = TRUE)
}

# draw the figure
fig_md_cola()

4.1.7 Four normalisations

restriction on \(A\) normalisation of \(\Gamma\) factors \(\mathbf f_t\)
Cholesky \(a_{12}=0\) ones on the diagonal the regressor and the residual
Symmetric root \(a_{12}=a_{21}\) ones on the diagonal each roommate’s own GPA
Structural the manual’s fuel flow one outside fact per factor headwind (km/h), load (t)
PCA first column longest columns of length one scores, in the units of the data

\(A=\Gamma D\): the diagonal \(D\) says how important each factor is, and \(\Gamma\) how the measured variables combine the factors. Choosing \(A\) needs a restriction; splitting it into \(\Gamma\) and \(D\) needs a normalisation.

PCA needs no outside information, neither an ordering of the variables nor a manual, which is one reason it is the most widely used. The rest of the chapter studies it.

Check your understanding
  1. In \(\mathbf x_t=\Gamma D\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\), the diagonal matrix \(D\)
    1. rotates the shocks
    2. scales each unit-variance shock into a factor in its own units
    3. holds the correlations of the variables
    4. is always the identity
  2. Measuring headwind in m/s instead of km/h changes
    1. the data
    2. \(A\)
    3. the split of \(A\) into \(\Gamma\) and \(D\), but not \(A\)
    4. nothing at all
  3. In the Cholesky split with ones on the diagonal of \(\Gamma\), the second factor is
    1. the second variable itself
    2. the part of the second variable not explained by the first, the regression residual
    3. the first principal component
    4. the peer effect
  4. With columns of \(\Gamma\) of length one, the factor variances \(d_j^2\)
    1. are all one
    2. add up to the total variance of the data
    3. are the correlations
    4. depend on the order of the variables
Answers 1 b. 2 c. 3 b. 4 b.

4.2 Two arrows, the first as long as possible

Which \(A\) does PCA pick? With Coke and Pepsi, the slider of the Introduction finds it.

4.2.1 Every rotation fits the data

Each week’s Coke and Pepsi sales (as deviations from the mean) are a combination of two uncorrelated shocks with variance one,

\[ \mathbf x_t=A\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t=\varepsilon_{t1}\,a_1+\varepsilon_{t2}\,a_2 , \]

where \(a_1\) and \(a_2\), the columns of \(A\), are the two arrows: what one standard deviation of each shock does to the two sales figures. Any \(A\) with \(AA'=S\) fits the data equally well (Section 1.3): turning both arrows together by an angle \(\varphi\) keeps their tips on the one-standard-deviation ellipse and leaves \(S\) unchanged. Algebraically, \(A(\varphi)=S^{1/2}Q(\varphi)\), with \(S^{1/2}\) the symmetric root and \(Q(\varphi)\) the rotation matrix of Section 3.7.

4.2.2 How much variance each arrow carries

One number summarises how much the data vary in all directions together: the total variance, the sum of the variances of the variables. It is the sum of the diagonal entries of \(S\), called the trace:

\[ \operatorname{tr}(S)=\operatorname{tr}\begin{pmatrix}s_1^2&s_{12}\\ s_{12}&s_2^2\end{pmatrix}=s_1^2+s_2^2 . \]

The covariance \(s_{12}\) is off the diagonal and does not enter. Now write each variance in terms of the arrows. Variable 1 is \(x_{t1}=a_{11}\varepsilon_{t1}+a_{12}\varepsilon_{t2}\), and the shocks are uncorrelated with variance one, so by the rule for linear combinations (Section 3.5.4)

\[ s_1^2=a_{11}^2\operatorname{var}(\varepsilon_{t1})+a_{12}^2\operatorname{var}(\varepsilon_{t2})+2a_{11}a_{12}\operatorname{cov}(\varepsilon_{t1},\varepsilon_{t2}) =a_{11}^2+a_{12}^2 , \]

and in the same way \(s_2^2=a_{21}^2+a_{22}^2\). Adding the two and regrouping the four squares by shock instead of by variable,

\[ \operatorname{tr}(S)=\underbrace{(a_{11}^2+a_{12}^2)}_{s_1^2}+\underbrace{(a_{21}^2+a_{22}^2)}_{s_2^2} =\underbrace{(a_{11}^2+a_{21}^2)}_{\lVert a_1\rVert^2}+\underbrace{(a_{12}^2+a_{22}^2)}_{\lVert a_2\rVert^2} . \]

The first grouping splits the total variance by variable, the second by shock: \(a_{11}^2+a_{21}^2\) collects what the first shock adds to the variance of each variable, and it is the squared length of the first column of \(A\), the first arrow.

The squared length of an arrow is the part of the total variance that its shock carries. The total is fixed by the data; the rotation only decides how it is divided. Turn the arrows with the slider:

fig_pca_arrows <- function() {
  S <- cov(cola); X <- scale(cola, scale = FALSE); root <- sym_root(S)
  phi_lab <- function(phi) sprintf("%.1f", phi)
  phi_grid <- sort(unique(c(seq(-90, 90, by = 2.5), pca_phi)))
  fk <- function(phi) factor(phi_lab(phi), levels = phi_lab(phi_grid))
  A_of <- function(phi) root %*% rotation_matrix(phi * pi / 180)
  len2 <- function(phi) colSums(A_of(phi)^2)
  cols <- c(col_a1, col_a2)
  arrows <- lapply(1:2, function(j) purrr::map_dfr(phi_grid, function(ph)
    arrow_geometry(A_of(ph)[, j], head_length = 0.2, head_width = 0.1, shaft_width = 0.022)$arrow |> mutate(k = fk(ph))))
  labs_df <- purrr::map_dfr(phi_grid, function(ph) { M <- A_of(ph); r <- sqrt(colSums(M^2))
    tibble(x = M[1, ] * (1 + 0.35 / r), y = M[2, ] * (1 + 0.35 / r), label = c("a<sub>1</sub>", "a<sub>2</sub>"),
           col = cols, k = fk(ph)) })
  ell <- ellipse_xy(root, 1)
  curve <- tibble(phi = seq(-90, 90, by = 0.5)) |>
    mutate(l1 = purrr::map_dbl(phi, ~ len2(.x)[1]), l2 = purrr::map_dbl(phi, ~ len2(.x)[2]))
  marks <- purrr::map_dfr(phi_grid, function(ph) { l <- len2(ph)
    tibble(phi = ph, l = l, col = cols, k = fk(ph)) })
  tot <- sum(diag(S))
  readout <- purrr::map_dfr(phi_grid, function(ph) { l <- len2(ph)
    tibble(x = 0, y = tot * 1.2, k = fk(ph),
           t = sprintf("‖a<sub>1</sub>‖² = %.2f (%.0f%%)    ‖a<sub>2</sub>‖² = %.2f (%.0f%%)    total = %.2f",
                       l[1], 100 * l[1] / tot, l[2], 100 * l[2] / tot, tot)) })

  p1 <- plot_ly() |>
    add_trace(x = X[, 1], y = X[, 2], type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
              marker = list(size = 5, color = "#6f7a8c", opacity = 0.4), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE) |>
    add_trace(x = ell[1, ], y = ell[2, ], type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = "black", width = 2),
              hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE)
  for (j in 1:2) p1 <- add_arrow_trace(p1, arrows[[j]], color = cols[j])
  p1 <- p1 |> add_trace(data = labs_df, x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~k, text = ~label, type = "scatter", mode = "text",
                        textfont = list(size = 16, color = ~col), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE)
  p2 <- plot_ly() |>
    add_trace(x = c(-90, 90), y = c(tot, tot), type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              line = list(color = "grey", dash = "dot"), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE) |>
    add_trace(x = -88, y = tot * 1.07, text = "total variance tr(S)", type = "scatter", mode = "text",
              textposition = "middle right", textfont = list(size = 11, color = "grey"), hoverinfo = "skip",
              showlegend = FALSE) |>
    add_trace(data = curve, x = ~phi, y = ~l1, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = col_a1, width = 2.5),
              hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE) |>
    add_trace(data = curve, x = ~phi, y = ~l2, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = col_a2, width = 2.5),
              hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE) |>
    add_trace(data = marks, x = ~phi, y = ~l, frame = ~k, type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
              marker = list(size = 12, color = ~col), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE) |>
    add_trace(data = readout, x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~k, text = ~t, type = "scatter", mode = "text",
              textfont = list(size = 12, color = "#2c3e50"), hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, inherit = FALSE)
  jump <- list(
    list(label = "PCA: first arrow longest", method = "animate",
         args = list(list(phi_lab(pca_phi)), list(mode = "immediate", frame = list(duration = 0, redraw = TRUE),
                                                   transition = list(duration = 0)))),
    list(label = "Symmetric root", method = "animate",
         args = list(list(phi_lab(0)), list(mode = "immediate", frame = list(duration = 0, redraw = TRUE),
                                            transition = list(duration = 0)))))
  subplot(p1, p2, widths = c(0.5, 0.5), margin = 0.07, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE) |>
    layout(xaxis  = list(title = "Coca-Cola sales (deviation)", range = c(-3.2, 3.2), zeroline = FALSE),
           yaxis  = list(title = "Pepsi sales (deviation)", range = c(-3.2, 3.2), scaleanchor = "x", zeroline = FALSE),
           xaxis2 = list(title = "rotation φ (degrees)", range = c(-90, 90), dtick = 45, zeroline = FALSE),
           yaxis2 = list(title = "variance carried by each arrow", range = c(0, tot * 1.3)),
           margin = list(t = 70, b = 150)) |>
    animation_opts(frame = 80, transition = 0, redraw = TRUE) |>
    animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "rotation φ = ", suffix = "°")) |>
    animation_button(x = 0, xanchor = "left", y = -0.3, yanchor = "top", label = "Play") |>
    finalize_animation(jump, start_frame = "0.0", prefix = "rotation φ = ", suffix = "°")
}

# draw the figure
fig_pca_arrows()

At \(\varphi=0\), the symmetric root, the two arrows carry nearly equal shares: a symmetric \(A\) has \(A'A=AA'=S\), so the squared arrow lengths equal the two variances, 1 and 1.1, or 48% and 52% of the total. As they turn, the blue arrow grows and the red one shrinks, until at \(\varphi\approx46\) degrees the blue arrow is as long as it can be:

Principal components analysis chooses the rotation at which the first arrow is longest, so that the first shock carries as much of the total variance as possible.

At that angle, \(\lVert a_1\rVert^2=2.00\), or 95% of the total, and \(\lVert a_2\rVert^2=0.10\). The two arrows are perpendicular and point along the axes of the ellipse: the long axis is the market (both brands up together), the short axis brand switching. These two directions are the principal components. With \(p\) variables there are \(p\) arrows, and the same idea continues: the first arrow as long as possible, then the second as long as possible given the first, and so on.

4.2.3 Scores: taking \(A\) apart one layer at a time

Split the PCA choice of \(A\) as in Section 4.1,

\[ A=\Gamma D=\begin{pmatrix}\gamma_1&\gamma_2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}d_1&0\\0&d_2\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}d_1\gamma_1&d_2\gamma_2\end{pmatrix}, \]

with the columns of \(\Gamma\) of length one. Column by column, each arrow is a length times a unit-length direction:

\[ a_j=d_j\,\gamma_j,\qquad d_j=\lVert a_j\rVert,\qquad \gamma_j=a_j/\lVert a_j\rVert , \]

and the factor variance \(d_j^2\) is the variance arrow \(j\) carries. Because the arrows are perpendicular, the columns of \(\Gamma\) are perpendicular unit vectors, \(\Gamma'\Gamma=I\): \(\Gamma\) is a rotation (possibly with a reflection), which turns space without stretching or squishing anything. Reading \(\mathbf x_t=\Gamma D\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) from right to left, one transformation after the other (3Blue1Brown, chapter 4): \(D\) stretches the round cloud of shocks along the axes (a diagonal matrix just scales each basis vector), and \(\Gamma\) turns the stretched cloud into place. The covariance matrix is \(S=AA'=\Gamma D^2\Gamma'\). The figure follows one week (orange) through the two steps; the arrows follow the two shocks, and the dashed lines show the week’s coordinates.

pca_step <- function(lab, col = "black") ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.05, xend = 0.95, y = 0.5, yend = 0.5, linewidth = 1.1, colour = col,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.63, label = lab, parse = TRUE, size = 5.5, colour = col) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) + theme_void()

shock_arrows <- function(B) tibble(x = B[1, ], y = B[2, ], col = c(col_a1, col_a2), lab = NA_character_, lx = 0, ly = 0)

cloud_pts <- function(X, alpha = 0.45) geom_point(data = tibble(x = X[, 1], y = X[, 2]), aes(x, y),
                                                   colour = "#6f7a8c", alpha = alpha, size = 1.5)

pca_panel <- function(P, Mell, Dcoord, week, title, sub, xl, yl, pc_lines = NULL, arrows_df = NULL, lim = c(-3.4, 3.4)) {
  col_wk <- "#e6820e"; pt <- P[week, ]
  el <- ellipse_xy(Mell, 1)
  c1 <- sum(pt * Dcoord[, 1]) * Dcoord[, 1]; c2 <- sum(pt * Dcoord[, 2]) * Dcoord[, 2]
  g <- ggplot() + axes0
  if (!is.null(pc_lines)) g <- g + geom_abline(slope = pc_lines[2, ] / pc_lines[1, ], intercept = 0,
                                               colour = c(col_a1, col_a2), alpha = 0.3)
  g <- g + cloud_pts(P, 0.35) + geom_path(data = tibble(x = el[1, ], y = el[2, ]), aes(x, y), linewidth = 0.8)
  if (!is.null(arrows_df)) g <- g +
    geom_segment(data = arrows_df, aes(0, 0, xend = x, yend = y, colour = I(col)), linewidth = 1.3,
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
    geom_label(data = filter(arrows_df, !is.na(lab)), aes(x * 1.18 + lx, y * 1.18 + ly, label = lab, colour = I(col)),
               size = 3.4, fontface = "bold", label.size = 0, fill = alpha("white", 0.8))
  g + geom_segment(aes(x = pt[1], y = pt[2], xend = c1[1], yend = c1[2]), linetype = "22", colour = col_wk) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = pt[1], y = pt[2], xend = c2[1], yend = c2[2]), linetype = "22", colour = col_wk) +
    geom_point(aes(x = pt[1], y = pt[2]), colour = col_wk, size = 3.2) +
    coord_equal(xlim = lim, ylim = lim) + labs(title = title, subtitle = sub, x = xl, y = yl)
}

pca_layers <- function() {
  X <- scale(cola, scale = FALSE); e <- eigen(cov(X), symmetric = TRUE)
  G <- e$vectors; if (G[1, 1] < 0) G[, 1] <- -G[, 1]; if (det(G) < 0) G[, 2] <- -G[, 2]
  D <- diag(sqrt(e$values)); Fs <- X %*% G; E <- sweep(Fs, 2, sqrt(e$values), "/")
  list(X = X, G = G, D = D, Fs = Fs, E = E, week = which.min((E[, 1] - 1.3)^2 + (E[, 2] - 1.6)^2))
}

fig_pca_forward <- function() {
  L <- pca_layers()
  p1 <- pca_panel(L$E, diag(2), diag(2), L$week, expression("Shocks "*bold(epsilon)[t]), "variance 1: round",
                  expression(epsilon[1]*" (market)"), expression(epsilon[2]*" (brand switching)"),
                  arrows_df = shock_arrows(diag(2)))
  p2 <- pca_panel(L$Fs, L$D, diag(2), L$week, expression("Scores "*bold(f)[t] == italic(D)*bold(epsilon)[t]),
                  "stretched along the axes", expression(italic(f)[1]), expression(italic(f)[2]),
                  arrows_df = shock_arrows(L$D))
  p3 <- pca_panel(L$X, L$G %*% L$D, diag(2), L$week, expression("Data "*bold(x)[t] == Gamma*bold(f)[t]*" = "*Gamma*italic(D)*bold(epsilon)[t]*" = "*italic(A)*bold(epsilon)[t]),
                  "rotated into place", "Coca-Cola (deviation)", "Pepsi (deviation)",
                  arrows_df = shock_arrows(L$G %*% L$D))
  p1 + pca_step("italic(D)") + p2 + pca_step("Gamma") + p3 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 0.2, 1, 0.2, 1))
}

# draw the figure
fig_pca_forward()

The scores go back from the data to the shocks. Undoing a product of transformations means undoing the last one first, so

\[ A^{-1}=\big(\Gamma D\big)^{-1}=D^{-1}\,\Gamma' , \]

where a rotation is undone by its transpose. Indeed, \(\Gamma'\Gamma=I\) says that applying \(\Gamma\) and then \(\Gamma'\) changes nothing, so \(\Gamma'\) is the inverse of \(\Gamma\), \(\Gamma^{-1}=\Gamma'\) (for a square matrix, a matrix that undoes it from one side also undoes it from the other, so \(\Gamma\Gamma'=I\) as well). The two layers come off one at a time:

  1. Undo the rotation. Turning the data back gives the factors, the principal component scores, \[ \mathbf f_t=\Gamma'\mathbf x_t,\qquad f_{tj}=\gamma_j'\mathbf x_t . \] Each score is an inner product with a unit vector, so it is the signed length of the projection of the week onto the direction of arrow \(j\) (3Blue1Brown, chapter 9). Put differently, \(\Gamma'\) is a change of basis (3Blue1Brown, chapter 13): \(\mathbf f_t\) describes the same week in coordinates whose axes are the arrows. The stretch is still in: the scores on component \(j\) have variance \(d_j^2\).
  2. Undo the stretch. Dividing each score by its standard deviation gives the shocks back, \[ \boldsymbol\varepsilon_t=D^{-1}\mathbf f_t,\qquad \varepsilon_{tj}=f_{tj}/d_j, \] the standardised scores, with variance one.

The second figure runs the same week backwards, from the data to the shocks. This time the purple arrows follow the two variables: in the data panel they are the axes, one unit of Coca-Cola and one unit of Pepsi. The dashed lines in the data panel run perpendicular to the two components: the scores are projections.

pca_step <- function(lab, col = "black") ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.05, xend = 0.95, y = 0.5, yend = 0.5, linewidth = 1.1, colour = col,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.63, label = lab, parse = TRUE, size = 5.5, colour = col) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) + theme_void()

cloud_pts <- function(X, alpha = 0.45) geom_point(data = tibble(x = X[, 1], y = X[, 2]), aes(x, y),
                                                   colour = "#6f7a8c", alpha = alpha, size = 1.5)

pca_panel <- function(P, Mell, Dcoord, week, title, sub, xl, yl, pc_lines = NULL, arrows_df = NULL, lim = c(-3.4, 3.4)) {
  col_wk <- "#e6820e"; pt <- P[week, ]

  c1 <- sum(pt * Dcoord[, 1]) * Dcoord[, 1]; c2 <- sum(pt * Dcoord[, 2]) * Dcoord[, 2]
  g <- ggplot() + axes0
  if (!is.null(pc_lines)) g <- g + geom_abline(slope = pc_lines[2, ] / pc_lines[1, ], intercept = 0,
                                               colour = c(col_a1, col_a2), alpha = 0.3)
  g <- g + cloud_pts(P, 0.35) + geom_path(data = tibble(x = el[1, ], y = el[2, ]), aes(x, y), linewidth = 0.8)

    geom_segment(data = arrows_df, aes(0, 0, xend = x, yend = y, colour = I(col)), linewidth = 1.3,

    geom_label(data = filter(arrows_df, !is.na(lab)), aes(x * 1.18 + lx, y * 1.18 + ly, label = lab, colour = I(col)),

pca_layers <- function() {
  X <- scale(cola, scale = FALSE); e <- eigen(cov(X), symmetric = TRUE)
  G <- e$vectors; if (G[1, 1] < 0) G[, 1] <- -G[, 1]; if (det(G) < 0) G[, 2] <- -G[, 2]
  D <- diag(sqrt(e$values)); Fs <- X %*% G; E <- sweep(Fs, 2, sqrt(e$values), "/")
